verses.title: The LORD upholds
verses.heading: Strength for the righteous
verses.meaning: Arms stand for the strength by which the wicked impose their will. That power will be broken, while the LORD sustains those who live rightly. The contrast follows the judgment about possessions in verse 16: apparent strength and abundance are less secure than God's care. Upholding does not mean that the righteous never stumble or suffer; it locates their hope in God's support rather than domination.
verses.context: Isaiah 41:8–12 addresses Israel, God's chosen servant, with a promise of strengthening and upholding amid hostile opposition. Psalm 145:14 praises the LORD for lifting those bowed down, while Psalm 63:6–10 sets sustaining care beside danger from enemies. The hand imagery in these poems speaks of divine power and help rather than supplying a bodily portrait of God.
explore: The image concerns the collapse of oppressive power. It gives readers no command to injure anyone.
God sustains those who trust Him. Their security rests in His care rather than superior force.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to uphold you today, when your own strength feels thin?
verses.alt: An old tree bent by wind is held up by a strong stone wall.

verses.title: He knows their days
verses.heading: God watches over the blameless
verses.meaning: The LORD knows the days of people who walk with integrity. Here knowing carries the warmth of attentive care: their lives are not overlooked when wrongdoing seems successful. Their enduring inheritance contrasts with the passing strength of the wicked. Blameless describes wholehearted integrity, not a claim that these people have never sinned, and the promise is larger than an easy present life.
verses.context: Psalm 1:4–6 contrasts God's guarding of the righteous path with the wicked way that perishes. Psalm 139:14–18 speaks of a life known by God before birth. Much later, 1 Peter 1:3–9 describes an unfading inheritance through Christ's resurrection while openly acknowledging grief and trials; that Christian setting remains distinct from Psalm 37.
explore: Each day is known within God's attentive care. A life hidden from public notice is not hidden from Him.
The promised future endures beyond passing appearances. It is received from God rather than seized.
verses.reflect: How does it feel to know God watches over every one of your days?
verses.alt: A plain stone sundial casts a quiet shadow in a garden, suggesting days held within attentive care.

verses.title: Satisfied in famine
verses.heading: Provision in hard times
verses.meaning: The poem expresses confidence that God will sustain His people through calamity and famine, so their trust will not finally end in disgrace. Read within this wisdom psalm, the promise directs hope toward God's faithful care rather than giving a test by which to judge hungry people. Scripture also records faithful people suffering need; this verse calls for trust and generosity, not blame or a guarantee of immediate abundance.
verses.context: In 1 Kings 17:12–16, the widow at Zarephath receives a specific promise through Elijah about flour and oil; it is a distinct narrative, not Psalm 37's stated occasion. Psalm 33:18–21 also trusts God's preservation in famine. Philippians 4:10–19 places God's provision beside Paul's experience of hunger, contentment and the Philippians' practical gifts.
explore: The poem trusts that reliance on God will be vindicated. Present suffering is not evidence of failed faith.
Provision is received as God's care. This hope also moves readers to share food with those in need.
verses.reflect: When resources are scarce, what helps you ask for support, share what you can, and entrust your needs to God?
verses.alt: Hands share a small loaf beside a modest bowl and oil jug, with dry fields beyond an open doorway.

verses.title: Like smoke
verses.heading: The fading glory of the wicked
verses.meaning: The apparent glory of the wicked is set beside the beauty of a field that fades and smoke that disperses. What seems impressive cannot secure lasting power against the LORD. The images support the opening warning against envy: a dazzling present is no measure of an enduring future. The poem describes judgment on evil without making every fading flower or afflicted person a sign of wickedness.
verses.context: Hosea 13:1–5 uses mist, dew, chaff and smoke to announce judgment on Ephraim's idolatry. James 4:13–16 uses vanishing mist to challenge human boasting about tomorrow. Psalm 102:1–5 uses smoke in an afflicted person's lament, showing that a similar image can describe innocent suffering as well as judgment; the settings must not be confused.
explore: A field's splendor can pass quickly. Outward brilliance does not establish lasting security.
Smoke thins and disappears. The image exposes the fragility of power set against the LORD.
verses.reflect: What impressive things around you are actually as fleeting as smoke?
verses.alt: Smoke drifts and fades from a dying fire over a field of wilting wildflowers.
